Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables

lessons.title: Develop a common vision
lessons.summary: A shared vision tells everyone why the project exists and what success looks like, so daily decisions pull in the same direction.
body: A common vision is a short, memorable description of the future state the project will create and the value it brings. It is not the scope statement; it is the 'why' behind the scope.
Build it with the people who will deliver and use the outcome, not for them. Co-creation builds ownership.
- Start from the business case and the sponsor's objectives.
- Run a workshop: product vision box, elevator pitch, or 'press release from the future'.
- Test the vision against stakeholder needs and constraints, then publish it where the team sees it every day.
Revisit the vision at key points (release planning, phase gates, major change requests). If the environment changes, update the vision openly rather than letting it silently drift.

keyTerms.definition: A concise statement of who the product is for, the need it meets and why it is better than alternatives.
The document that formally authorizes the project and links it to organizational objectives.
One outcome measure the team uses to judge whether work moves toward the vision.

lessons.example: A hospital IT team argued about which features to build first. The project manager facilitated a two-hour session with nurses and the sponsor to write a one-sentence vision: 'Nurses spend ten more minutes per shift with patients.' Feature debates were then settled by asking which item moved that number most.
lessons.approachNote: Predictive projects capture the vision in the charter and business case. Agile teams make it visible in a product vision and refresh it each release; the product owner is its day-to-day guardian.
lessons.examTip: When a question describes a team pulling in different directions, the best answer usually re-connects people to the shared vision and objectives before any directive action.

lessons.title: Manage conflicts
lessons.summary: Conflict is normal and can be useful; the project manager's job is to address its source early and collaboratively.
body: Common sources of project conflict are schedules, priorities, resources, technical opinions, procedures, cost and personalities.
Five classic resolution approaches:
- Collaborate / problem-solve: work together on the underlying issue; usually the best long-term result.
- Compromise / reconcile: each side gives something up; acceptable when collaboration is not possible.
- Smooth / accommodate: emphasize agreement; preserves relationships short-term.
- Force / direct: one view wins; reserved for emergencies, safety or legal issues.
- Withdraw / avoid: step back; useful only to let emotions cool or when the issue is trivial.

Assess the stage of the conflict (from problem to solve, through disagreement, contest and crusade, to world war). The higher it escalates, the more structured and protective the intervention must be. Address conflict privately first and focus on interests, not positions.

keyTerms.definition: Incorporating multiple viewpoints to reach consensus and commitment.
Team-created agreements on values, decision-making and conflict handling.
A shared belief that people can speak up without fear of punishment or humiliation.

lessons.example: Two senior developers disagree loudly in the stand-up about an architecture choice. The project manager thanks both, ends the stand-up on time, then meets them together with the architect to list each option's trade-offs against agreed criteria.
lessons.approachNote: In agile teams the team charter and retrospectives are the first tools; the servant leader coaches the team to resolve conflict itself. In predictive projects the project manager more often facilitates directly, but collaboration is still preferred.
lessons.examTip: Look for answers where the PM meets the parties, listens and facilitates a collaborative solution. 'Escalate to the sponsor' or 'force a decision' are rarely first steps.

lessons.title: Lead the project team
lessons.summary: Leading the team means creating the conditions for people to do their best work: clear goals, support, autonomy and growth.
body: Modern project leadership is mostly servant leadership: remove obstacles, shield the team from disruption, and grow capability.
- Set direction: link work to the vision and outcomes.
- Build the team: onboarding, team charter, clear roles (a RACI helps in predictive settings).
- Empower: let the team decide how to do the work; agree decision boundaries.
- Develop: coaching, mentoring, training and recognition.
- Adapt style: directive for a new team, supportive or delegating as maturity grows (situational leadership).
Emotional intelligence underpins all of this: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and relationship management. Recognize contributions publicly and give corrective feedback privately.
AI tools are changing team work. Leaders set norms for responsible use, such as checking AI output, protecting confidential data and keeping humans accountable for decisions.

keyTerms.definition: Leading by serving the team's needs, removing impediments and enabling self-organization.
Adapting leadership style to the competence and commitment of the individual or team.
The ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and those of others.

lessons.example: A newly formed team keeps missing sprint goals. Instead of assigning tasks, the project manager runs a working-agreements session, pairs a junior developer with a senior one, and asks the team what blocks them; the top blocker (slow test environment) is fixed within a week.
lessons.approachNote: Agile: the team self-organizes; the PM/scrum master coaches. Predictive: the PM plans resources and assignments but should still empower and develop people.
lessons.examTip: Prefer answers that empower, coach and support the team over answers that micromanage, blame or replace people.

lessons.title: Engage stakeholders
lessons.summary: Stakeholder engagement starts with finding everyone who can affect or is affected by the project, then involving them at the right level.
body: Identify stakeholders early and continuously; new ones appear throughout the project.
Analyze them with tools such as a power/interest grid, salience model or influence/impact grid.
Assess current versus desired engagement (unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading) in a stakeholder engagement assessment matrix.
Plan engagement actions that close the gap, for example demos for neutral users or one-to-one meetings with resistant managers.
The July 2026 outline puts greater emphasis on stakeholder engagement and on outcomes for stakeholders, including sustainability and social impact.

keyTerms.definition: A list of stakeholders with their role, interest, influence and engagement information.
Groups stakeholders as manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed or monitor.
Compares current (C) and desired (D) engagement levels per stakeholder.

lessons.example: During a warehouse automation project the PM noticed the union representative was missing from the register. Adding them early and inviting them to design workshops avoided a later dispute about shift patterns.
lessons.approachNote: Agile teams engage stakeholders through frequent reviews and demos. Predictive projects rely more on planned communications and formal reviews, but both need ongoing engagement.
lessons.examTip: If a 'new' or 'overlooked' stakeholder appears in a question, the first step is usually to update the stakeholder register and analyze them.

lessons.title: Align stakeholder expectations
lessons.summary: Alignment means stakeholders agree on objectives, priorities and success criteria before major work commits resources.
body: Misaligned expectations are a leading cause of project failure. Make expectations explicit early.
- Clarify objectives, acceptance criteria and constraints in the charter or product vision.
- Prioritize together using MoSCoW, value-versus-effort or weighted scoring.
- Resolve conflicting requirements by returning to business objectives, and escalate genuine trade-offs to the sponsor or product owner with options.
- Record agreements: requirements documents, definition of done, service-level targets.
Alignment is a facilitation task: bring the parties together rather than shuttling messages between them.

keyTerms.definition: Prioritization into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time.
Conditions a deliverable must meet to be accepted.
The team's shared checklist for when an increment is complete.

lessons.example: Marketing wanted a launch in March; compliance needed an audit trail that would take until May. The PM ran a joint session that agreed a March pilot for internal users with the audit trail as a must-have for the May public launch.
lessons.approachNote: Agile: the product owner aligns stakeholders through the backlog. Predictive: alignment is captured in baselined requirements and the scope statement.
lessons.examTip: Choose answers that bring conflicting stakeholders together around business objectives, rather than siding with the most senior person.

lessons.title: Manage stakeholder expectations
lessons.summary: Expectations shift during a project; the PM monitors them and responds before small gaps become crises.
body: Monitor engagement and sentiment through conversations, surveys, demos and the issue log.
- Communicate bad news early with facts, impact and options.
- Use the issue log to track concerns to resolution.
- Re-plan engagement when a stakeholder's power, interest or attitude changes.
- Celebrate delivered value so stakeholders see progress.
Never hide problems to keep stakeholders 'happy'. Transparency builds trust over time.

keyTerms.definition: A record of current problems, owners and resolution dates.
Strategies and actions to involve stakeholders effectively.
Openly sharing status, risks and decisions.

lessons.example: A sponsor expected a mobile app to support offline mode, but it was never in scope. Spotting this in a demo, the PM explained the current scope, estimated the change and let the sponsor decide via change control.
lessons.approachNote: Agile: frequent demos reveal expectation gaps quickly. Predictive: gaps often surface at milestone reviews, so proactive check-ins matter more.
lessons.examTip: When a stakeholder is unhappy, first understand their concern (meet, listen) and check the plan and register. Then act.

lessons.title: Help ensure knowledge transfer
lessons.summary: Knowledge transfer makes sure what the team learns stays with the organization and reaches the people who will operate the outcome.
body: Two kinds of knowledge: explicit knowledge (documents, code, procedures), which is easy to codify, and tacit knowledge (experience, judgment), which spreads through people.
- Explicit tools: lessons-learned register, wikis, runbooks, knowledge bases.
- Tacit tools: pairing, mentoring, communities of practice, job shadowing, storytelling.
Capture lessons throughout the project, not only at the end. Plan handover to operations and support teams early, including training and documentation.

keyTerms.definition: A living record of what worked, what didn't and recommendations, kept throughout the project.
Personal know-how that is hard to write down.
A group sharing expertise on a topic across projects.

lessons.example: Before a key engineer rotated off, the PM scheduled two weeks of pairing with her successor and recorded short videos of the deployment process for the support team.
lessons.approachNote: Agile teams share knowledge through pairing, mob programming and retrospectives. Predictive projects formalize lessons learned at phase ends, but should record them continuously.
lessons.examTip: Answers that update the lessons-learned register promptly or arrange pairing/mentoring are usually stronger than 'document it at closure'.

lessons.title: Plan and manage communication
lessons.summary: Communication planning decides who needs what information, when, in what format and through which channel, and checks that it worked.
body: Start from stakeholder analysis: needs differ between a sponsor, a regulator and an end user.
Number of communication channels = n(n-1)/2, where n is the number of people. Adding people grows complexity fast.
- Push communication: emails, reports (sent to recipients).
- Pull communication: intranet, dashboards (recipients fetch it).
- Interactive communication: meetings, calls, workshops (best for complex or sensitive topics).

Check effectiveness through feedback. Adjust language, culture, time zone and accessibility needs. Information radiators such as burndown charts and Kanban boards make status visible without extra meetings.

keyTerms.definition: Defines how project information is collected, distributed and controlled.
A visible display of key project information, physical or digital.
n(n-1)/2 potential paths between n people.

lessons.example: A distributed team across India, Germany and Brazil missed decisions made in calls. The PM moved decisions to a shared decision log (pull), rotated meeting times fairly, and kept an interactive weekly sync for complex topics.
lessons.approachNote: Agile relies on face-to-face or video conversation and information radiators; predictive plans more formal reporting. Hybrid often uses both.
lessons.examTip: If a stakeholder says they are not getting information, review the communications management plan before choosing a new tool.

lessons.title: Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery
lessons.summary: The integrated plan pulls together how scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, risk and stakeholders will be managed, and chooses the delivery approach.
body: Integration is the project manager's core responsibility: making the parts of the plan consistent with each other.
- Choose the development approach (predictive, adaptive or hybrid) by assessing requirement certainty, stakeholder availability, risk, regulation and organizational culture.
- Tailor processes to the project; do not apply every tool by default.
- Set baselines (scope, schedule, cost) in predictive work. Agile uses a roadmap, release plan and backlog instead.
- Define how the plan will be updated and approved.
The kickoff meeting launches execution and aligns the team and stakeholders on the plan.

keyTerms.definition: Adapting processes, tools and artifacts to fit the project context.
The integrated scope, schedule and cost baselines used to measure performance.
Combining predictive and adaptive elements, e.g. predictive hardware with agile software.

lessons.example: A medical-device project used a predictive plan for regulatory hardware milestones and two-week sprints for the companion app, integrated through a shared milestone roadmap.
lessons.approachNote: The exam uses a mix of about 40% predictive and 60% agile or hybrid items. Expect questions asking which approach fits a scenario.
lessons.examTip: When choosing an approach: high uncertainty and frequent feedback point to agile; fixed regulatory requirements and stable scope point to predictive; mixed points to hybrid.

lessons.title: Develop and manage project scope
lessons.summary: Scope management defines and controls what is and is not included, whether as a baselined WBS or a prioritized backlog.
body: Predictive: collect requirements, create the scope statement, decompose work into a WBS down to work packages, and baseline it (scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary).
Adaptive: capture needs as a product backlog of user stories, refined continuously and prioritized by value.
- Validate scope: the customer formally accepts deliverables.
- Control scope: manage changes and prevent scope creep (uncontrolled changes) and gold plating (adding extras nobody asked for).
- Requirements traceability matrix: links requirements to objectives and deliverables.

keyTerms.definition: Hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work.
Uncontrolled expansion of scope without adjustments to time, cost and resources.
An ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product.

lessons.example: A developer added a 'nice' animation that the client never asked for, which delayed testing by two days: that is gold plating. The PM reminded the team to work only on approved scope and logged the idea for the product owner to consider.
lessons.approachNote: In agile, scope is variable within fixed time and cost (timeboxes). In predictive, scope is fixed and changes go through change control.
lessons.examTip: Validate scope means customer acceptance; control quality means correctness. Questions often test this difference.

lessons.title: Help ensure value-based delivery
lessons.summary: Value-based delivery means sequencing work to deliver the greatest business value early and measuring outcomes, not just outputs.
body: Value can be financial, social, environmental or strategic. Benefits are realized when outcomes are used.
- Deliver incrementally: an MVP or minimum marketable feature gets feedback and value early.
- Prioritize by value against cost and risk; reprioritize as you learn.
- Measure outcomes with KPIs and benefits realization plans.
- Stop or pivot work that no longer delivers value.
The July 2026 outline stresses outcomes, value and business impact over pure output.

keyTerms.definition: Minimum viable product: the smallest release that tests a value hypothesis.
Describes how and when benefits will be delivered and measured.
Output is what you produce; outcome is the change it creates.

lessons.example: Instead of building all twelve reporting screens, the team released the two that managers used daily. Usage data then showed that four planned screens were unnecessary.
lessons.approachNote: Agile embeds value delivery in every iteration. Predictive projects realize value at the end unless phased releases are planned.
lessons.examTip: Prefer answers that deliver early value and gather feedback over answers that wait until everything is complete.

lessons.title: Plan and manage resources
lessons.summary: Resource management plans, acquires and manages the people, equipment, materials and facilities the project needs.
body: - Estimate resource needs per activity or story; consider skills, availability and calendars.
- Acquire resources: negotiate with functional managers, use pre-assignment, or source virtual and remote team members.
- Resource levelling adjusts start and finish dates to fit limited resources and can lengthen the critical path. Resource smoothing stays within float.
- Physical resources: plan lead times, logistics and just-in-time delivery.
- Track utilization and resolve over-allocation.

keyTerms.definition: Adjusting dates to balance demand with supply; may change the critical path.
Adjusting activities within free and total float; does not change the critical path.
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed assignment matrix.

lessons.example: A shared database expert was booked on two projects in the same week. The PM met the other PM and the functional manager, re-sequenced non-critical work, and agreed a split schedule.
lessons.approachNote: Agile teams are ideally dedicated, stable and cross-functional. Predictive projects often borrow resources from functional managers.
lessons.examTip: Over-allocated key person? Look for negotiation with the functional manager and re-planning, not unilateral overtime.

lessons.title: Plan and manage procurement
lessons.summary: Procurement covers deciding what to buy, choosing the right contract type, selecting sellers fairly and managing the agreement through closure.
body: - Make-or-buy analysis: compare cost, capability, risk and strategic fit.
- Fixed price (FFP, FPIF): seller carries the most cost risk; needs a well-defined scope.
- Cost-reimbursable (CPFF, CPIF, CPAF): buyer carries the most cost risk; suits uncertain scope.
- Time and materials: hybrid; good for small or uncertain work, so cap it with a not-to-exceed amount.

Procurement documents include the statement of work and RFP/RFQ/RFI. Select sellers with weighted source-selection criteria. Manage the contract: inspections, payments, claims and changes only through the contract's change process. Agile contracts can use capped T&M, fixed-price increments or 'money for nothing, change for free' clauses.

keyTerms.definition: Description of the products or services to be procured.
A contested change where the buyer and seller disagree on compensation.
Only the parties to a contract have rights and obligations under it.

lessons.example: Scope for a new data platform was uncertain, so the buyer chose a cost-plus-incentive-fee contract with clear performance metrics instead of fixed price.
lessons.approachNote: Agile procurement favours collaboration, incremental delivery and flexible scope within budget caps.
lessons.examTip: Who carries the risk? Fixed price: seller. Cost-reimbursable: buyer. Disputes are resolved per the contract terms, ideally by negotiation first.

lessons.title: Plan and manage finance
lessons.summary: Financial management estimates costs, sets a budget with reserves, and tracks spending and value with methods such as earned value.
body: - Estimating: analogous, parametric, bottom-up, three-point (PERT: (O + 4M + P) / 6).
- Budget = cost baseline + management reserve. Contingency reserves for known risks are inside the baseline; management reserve for unknown risks is outside it and needs approval to use.
- Earned value: PV (planned value), EV (earned value), AC (actual cost).
- CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV; CPI = EV / AC; SPI = EV / PV.
- EAC (typical) = BAC / CPI; ETC = EAC − AC; VAC = BAC − EAC; TCPI = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC).
CPI or SPI below 1 means over budget or behind schedule.

keyTerms.definition: Budget at completion: total planned value.
Budget withheld for unknown-unknowns; not in the cost baseline.
Aligning planned spending with funding constraints.

lessons.example: BAC = 100,000; EV = 40,000; AC = 50,000; PV = 45,000. CPI = 0.8 and SPI ≈ 0.89, so the project is over budget and behind schedule. EAC = 100,000 / 0.8 = 125,000.
lessons.approachNote: Agile projects often track cost per iteration and burn rate; cost is relatively fixed by team size and timebox.
lessons.examTip: Memorize: 'EV first' in the variance and index formulas. Negative variance or an index below 1 is bad.

lessons.title: Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
lessons.summary: Quality management plans how to meet requirements and prevents defects, rather than relying only on finding them.
body: - Quality vs grade: low quality is always a problem; low grade (fewer features) may be acceptable.
- Cost of quality: prevention + appraisal (conformance) versus internal + external failure (non-conformance). Prevention is cheapest.
- Manage quality (assurance): process audits and improvement. Control quality: inspect and test deliverables.
- Tools: control charts (the rule of seven, limits), Pareto charts (80/20), fishbone diagrams, checklists, statistical sampling.
Agile builds quality in through the definition of done, automated tests, continuous integration and frequent reviews.

keyTerms.definition: Total cost of conformance and non-conformance over the product life.
Boundaries of common-cause variation on a control chart (typically ±3σ).
Control quality verifies correctness; validate scope gains customer acceptance.

lessons.example: A Pareto analysis of help-desk tickets showed that three defect types caused 78% of complaints. The team fixed those first.
lessons.approachNote: Agile: quality is everyone's job every sprint. Predictive: a quality management plan defines metrics, audits and inspections.
lessons.examTip: Seven consecutive points on one side of the mean is a signal of a non-random pattern even inside the control limits.

lessons.title: Plan and manage schedule
lessons.summary: Schedule management sequences work, estimates durations, finds the critical path and keeps delivery on track.
body: - Define and sequence activities (FS, SS, FF, SF dependencies; leads and lags).
- Critical path: the longest path through the network; zero total float. A delay on it delays the project.
- Compression: crashing adds resources (adds cost); fast tracking overlaps activities (adds risk).
- Agile scheduling: timeboxed iterations, velocity-based release planning and burndown or burnup charts.
Float (slack) = LS − ES or LF − EF.

keyTerms.definition: The sequence of activities that determines the shortest project duration.
Doing activities in parallel that were planned in sequence.
Amount of work a team completes per iteration, used for forecasting.

lessons.example: To recover two weeks, the team began interior wiring before all walls were inspected (fast tracking), accepting some rework risk after discussing it with the sponsor.
lessons.approachNote: Predictive: schedule baseline and critical path. Agile: fixed cadence, forecast scope using velocity.
lessons.examTip: Crashing costs money; fast tracking adds risk. Only compress activities on the critical path.

lessons.title: Evaluate project status
lessons.summary: Evaluating status compares actual performance with plans and outcomes and communicates it honestly so decisions can be made.
body: - Predictive: variance analysis, earned value, milestone tracking and the schedule baseline.
- Agile: burndown and burnup charts, velocity trends, cumulative flow diagrams and sprint reviews.
- Use KPIs that reflect outcomes (adoption, satisfaction) as well as delivery.
- Forecast completion and highlight trends, not just current numbers.
Dashboards and information radiators make status transparent. 'Watermelon reporting' (green outside, red inside) erodes trust.

keyTerms.definition: Shows work completed against total scope over time.
Shows work items in each state over time, revealing bottlenecks.
Explaining differences between planned and actual performance.

lessons.example: A cumulative flow diagram showed the 'testing' band widening every week. The team limited work in progress and paired developers with testers, and flow recovered.
lessons.approachNote: Agile status is visible daily; predictive status is often reported at intervals against baselines.
lessons.examTip: If metrics and reality disagree, investigate root causes before reporting or re-baselining.

lessons.title: Manage project closure
lessons.summary: Closure confirms acceptance, transfers outcomes, releases resources, closes contracts and captures lessons, including for terminated projects.
body: - Obtain formal acceptance of final deliverables.
- Transition to operations: training, documentation, support agreements.
- Close procurements: verify all work is complete and settle claims.
- Finalize the lessons-learned register and archive records.
- Release and recognize the team.
- Confirm benefits measurement will continue after the project ends.
Even a cancelled project goes through closure to capture knowledge and close obligations.

keyTerms.definition: Summary of performance, achievements and variances at closure.
How deliverables move to operational ownership.
Collecting records, archiving and releasing resources.

lessons.example: The sponsor cancelled a project after a merger. The PM still documented work completed, closed vendor contracts, archived code and ran a lessons-learned session.
lessons.approachNote: Agile products may never 'close'; releases end, and teams move on. Project closure still applies to funding and contracts.
lessons.examTip: Before closing, confirm acceptance and close all contracts. Lessons learned are captured even when projects are terminated.

lessons.title: Define and establish project governance
lessons.summary: Governance defines who decides what, how decisions are escalated, and how the project stays aligned with organizational strategy.
body: - Governance framework: roles (sponsor, steering committee, PMO, product owner), decision rights, phase gates and escalation paths.
- Organizational structures (functional, matrix, projectized) affect the PM's authority.
- The PMO may be supportive, controlling or directive.
- Adaptive governance uses lightweight, frequent decision points: backlog reviews and portfolio Kanban.
Good governance is proportional: enough control for risk and compliance, not so much that it blocks delivery.

keyTerms.definition: Senior group that provides direction and makes key decisions.
A review at the end of a phase to decide whether to continue, modify or stop.
Agreed route for raising decisions beyond the team's authority.

lessons.example: A decision about data residency stalled for weeks. The PM proposed a governance change: decisions under 50k were delegated to the product owner, and above that went to a fortnightly steering meeting with a 5-day decision target.
lessons.approachNote: Agile governance focuses on outcomes and transparency; predictive uses formal gates and baselines.
lessons.examTip: When a decision is above the PM's authority, follow the governance or escalation path rather than deciding alone.

lessons.title: Plan and manage project compliance
lessons.summary: Compliance makes sure the project and its outcomes meet legal, regulatory, contractual, security, privacy, accessibility and internal policy requirements.
body: - Identify applicable requirements early: industry regulation, data protection, safety, environmental and accessibility.
- Classify each requirement by consequence of non-compliance and plan how to meet it.
- Build compliance into acceptance criteria and the definition of done.
- Audit and track compliance, involving legal and compliance experts.
- Sustainability and ESG reporting obligations increasingly apply to projects.
Non-compliance is not a negotiable trade-off: escalate and stop if necessary.

keyTerms.definition: A requirement imposed by law or a regulator.
An independent check that processes and outputs meet obligations.
Environmental, social and governance criteria.

lessons.example: Midway through a CRM rollout, a new data privacy rule took effect. The PM engaged the privacy officer, added consent tracking to the backlog as a must-have, and updated the risk register.
lessons.approachNote: Agile teams embed compliance checks in the definition of done; predictive projects plan compliance activities and audits in the plan.
lessons.examTip: If a team member discovers non-compliance, the right answer addresses it immediately and transparently, never hiding it to meet a deadline.

lessons.title: Manage and control changes
lessons.summary: Change control evaluates, approves or rejects changes in a structured way so the impact on scope, schedule, cost, risk and value is understood.
body: Predictive change process:
- Log the change request.
- Analyze the impact on all constraints.
- Present options to the change control board (CCB) or authorized decision maker.
- Record the decision.
- Update plans and baselines, then communicate.
Adaptive: changes are welcomed and enter the product backlog; the product owner reprioritizes. Changes inside a sprint goal are negotiated with the team.
Configuration management controls versions of deliverables and documents.

keyTerms.definition: Group responsible for reviewing and approving change requests.
Controlling specifications and versions of deliverables.
Reviewing changes against all project constraints together.

lessons.example: A sponsor emailed the developer directly asking for a new report. The developer told the PM, who logged a change request, analyzed a 3-day impact and took it to the CCB, which approved it for the next release.
lessons.approachNote: Agile: the backlog absorbs change; predictive: formal change control protects the baselines.
lessons.examTip: Typical sequence: evaluate impact → submit to CCB → update plan → communicate. Never implement a change before approval in a predictive setting.

lessons.title: Remove impediments and manage issues
lessons.summary: Impediments and issues block progress; the project manager makes them visible, owns their resolution, and prevents recurrence.
body: - An issue is a current problem; a risk is an uncertain future event.
- Make impediments visible: stand-ups, impediment boards, the issue log.
- Prioritize by impact, assign owners and due dates, and follow up.
- Remove blockers within your control. Escalate those beyond it with facts and options.
- Analyze root causes (5 whys, fishbone) to stop repeats.

keyTerms.definition: Anything that slows or stops the team's progress.
Identifying the underlying reason a problem occurred.
An unplanned response to an issue that has occurred.

lessons.example: Developers waited 3 days for test-environment access each sprint. The scrum master escalated with data on lost hours; IT automated access requests, removing the impediment permanently.
lessons.approachNote: The scrum master or servant leader is the impediment remover in agile; in predictive, the PM manages the issue log.
lessons.examTip: Look for the servant leader removing the impediment for the team, not telling the team to work around it alone.

lessons.title: Plan and manage risk
lessons.summary: Risk management finds, analyzes and responds to uncertainty, both threats and opportunities, throughout the project.
body: - Identify risks continuously, using workshops, checklists, SWOT and assumption analysis.
- Qualitative analysis: probability and impact. Quantitative: expected monetary value (EMV = probability × impact), Monte Carlo, decision trees.
- Threat responses: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, escalate.
- Opportunity responses: exploit, share, enhance, accept, escalate.
- Assign risk owners and triggers. Monitor residual and secondary risks. Reserves fund responses.
AI tools bring new risks (bias, data leakage, hallucination) as well as opportunities (better forecasting).

keyTerms.definition: The degree of uncertainty an organization is willing to accept.
Person responsible for monitoring a risk and executing the response.
Risk remaining after responses are implemented.

lessons.example: A threat with 30% probability and a 50,000 cost impact has an EMV of -15,000. An opportunity with 20% probability and a 40,000 saving has an EMV of +8,000. The net contingency need is 7,000.
lessons.approachNote: Agile reduces risk through short iterations, early feedback and risk-adjusted backlogs; predictive uses a formal risk register and reserves.
lessons.examTip: If a risk occurs, implement the planned response (it's now an issue). If an unidentified risk occurs, apply a workaround and then update the registers.

lessons.title: Continuous improvement
lessons.summary: Continuous improvement uses feedback and data to improve processes, products and team performance throughout the project.
body: - Retrospectives at the end of each iteration or phase: what went well, what to improve, and one or two concrete actions.
- Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) and Kaizen: small, frequent improvements.
- Lean: eliminate waste, such as waiting, handoffs, over-processing, defects and partially done work.
- Use metrics such as cycle time and defect rates to verify improvement.
Share improvements across projects through the PMO and communities of practice.

keyTerms.definition: A regular meeting where the team reflects and agrees improvements.
Plan-Do-Check-Act improvement cycle.
Philosophy of continuous small improvements.

lessons.example: Retrospectives showed that code reviews waited an average of 2 days. The team agreed a 'review before starting new work' rule, and cycle time fell 30% in two sprints.
lessons.approachNote: Agile builds improvement into every iteration; predictive projects should still review lessons at phase ends and act on them, not just record them.
lessons.examTip: The best answer turns lessons into action now, not only for future projects.

lessons.title: Support organizational change
lessons.summary: Projects create change; supporting organizational change means helping people adopt new ways of working so benefits are realized.
body: - Assess change readiness and the impact on people, processes and culture.
- Use change models: ADKAR (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement), Kotter's 8 steps, Satir model of change.
- Engage change champions; communicate the why; train; and reinforce new behaviours.
- Plan for resistance as a normal reaction; listen to it, since it often contains useful information.
- Measure adoption to confirm the change sticks.

keyTerms.definition: Individual change model: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.
The organization's preparedness to accept and adopt change.
Influential person who promotes and supports the change locally.

lessons.example: A new procurement tool went live but staff kept using spreadsheets. The PM worked with team leaders as champions, ran short hands-on clinics and switched off the spreadsheet templates after a 4-week overlap.
lessons.approachNote: Agile's frequent releases reduce change shock; predictive 'big bang' deployments need more deliberate change management.
lessons.examTip: Low adoption after go-live points to change management (training, communication, reinforcement), not to a new technical solution.

lessons.title: Evaluate external business environment changes
lessons.summary: The external environment (market, regulation, technology, economy, society, environment) changes during the project; the PM watches for changes and adjusts.
body: - Scan regularly with PESTLE: political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental.
- Assess the impact on objectives, business case and risk register.
- Recommend adjusting scope, approach or even stopping the project when the business case no longer holds.
- Consider sustainability: carbon footprint, supply-chain ethics and community impact.
- Keep the sponsor informed so strategic decisions are made in time.

keyTerms.definition: Framework for analyzing external factors: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental.
Justification for the project, documenting expected benefits versus costs.
A significant external shift affecting product value.

lessons.example: A competitor launched a free version of the product being built. The PM organized a rapid impact assessment with the product owner and sponsor, who refocused the backlog on two differentiating features.
lessons.approachNote: Agile responds quickly via backlog reprioritization; predictive may need formal change requests and business-case revalidation.
lessons.examTip: When external change threatens the business case, assess the impact and inform the sponsor or governance body. Don't continue blindly or cancel unilaterally.
