faqs.question: Is this app made by PMI?
faqs.answer: No. OpenPM Prep is an independent, free study platform. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Project Management Institute (PMI). PMP, PMBOK and PMI are registered marks of Project Management Institute, Inc.

faqs.question: Which exam version does this app follow?
faqs.answer: The PMP exam launched in July 2026 (ECO-2026-07): People 33%, Process 41%, Business Environment 26%; 180 questions (170 scored, 10 unscored pretest) in 240 minutes, with two 10-minute breaks (after the case-study section and about halfway through the independent questions). Every lesson and question shows its ECO tag.

faqs.question: How many times can I take the exam?
faqs.answer: According to the PMI Certification Handbook, you can take the exam up to three times within your one-year eligibility period. After three attempts you must wait one year from the last attempt before reapplying.

faqs.question: Is everything really free?
faqs.answer: Yes. Registration, study material, practice tests, mock exams, results and basic assistance are free. There are no subscriptions, premium locks or paid exam packages.

faqs.question: What does the 'Demo content' label mean?
faqs.answer: Demo items were written for this app and have not yet been reviewed by a PMP-certified subject-matter expert. Reviewed items show 'Reviewed'. Both are original, but use demo items with that in mind.

faqs.question: Are these real exam questions?
faqs.answer: No. All questions are original practice items written against the public Exam Content Outline. Real PMP questions are confidential, and sharing them breaks PMI's rules.

faqs.question: How is the readiness score calculated?
faqs.answer: Readiness = 25% lesson coverage + 15% flashcard retention + 25% recent practice accuracy + 35% average of your last two full mocks. It is a study guide, not a pass prediction.

faqs.question: How are results banded?
faqs.answer: PMI score reports give a pass/fail result plus performance by domain. PMI sets its passing standard through psychometric analysis and does not publish a fixed passing percentage. This app's bands (Above Target, Target, Below Target, Needs Improvement at 80/65/50%) are its own estimate, not PMI's scoring.

faqs.question: Can I use the app offline?
faqs.answer: Yes. All lessons, flashcards and questions are on your device. Guest progress is stored on the device only.

faqs.question: How do breaks work in the full mock?
faqs.answer: Like the real exam: after the case-study section and about halfway through the independent questions you may take a 10-minute break. Once you start a break, you cannot go back to the previous section. The exam clock pauses during breaks.

faqs.question: How are multiple-response and drag-and-drop items scored?
faqs.answer: All-or-nothing, as on the real exam. The review screen shows which parts you got right so you can learn.

faqs.question: Do I still need 35 hours of training?
faqs.answer: Yes. You need at least 35 hours of project management training aligned with the Exam Content Outline. From 1 December 2026, live (instructor-led) hours count only if a PMI Authorized Training Partner, a China Registered Education Provider or an eligible accredited academic program delivers them. Self-paced courses with an end-of-course assessment can come from any provider. PMI states that books and practice exams alone are not accepted, so this app does not provide training hours.

faqs.question: Can institutions partner with the app?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use the partnership enquiry form in the Institutions section. Directory entries are 'Listed' public information only. A 'Verified partner' badge appears only after written authorization.

revision.definition: CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV. Negative = over budget / behind schedule.
CPI = EV / AC; SPI = EV / PV. Below 1 = bad.
EAC = BAC / CPI. Atypical: AC + (BAC − EV). With CPI×SPI: AC + (BAC − EV)/(CPI × SPI).
ETC = EAC − AC; VAC = BAC − EAC.
TCPI = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC) to meet BAC.
Total float = LS − ES = LF − EF. Critical path float = 0.
Crashing adds cost; fast tracking adds risk.
Fixed price: seller carries risk. Cost-reimbursable: buyer carries risk. T&M: shared; cap it.
Contingency (known-unknowns) is inside the cost baseline; management reserve (unknown-unknowns) is outside it.
Low quality is always a problem; low grade may be acceptable.
Control quality = correct (verified); validate scope = accepted by the customer.
Agile: fixed time and cost, flexible scope. Predictive: fixed scope with change control.
Threats: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, escalate. Opportunities: exploit, share, enhance, accept, escalate.

cases.title: Clinic appointment platform
cases.body: You lead a 9-person hybrid team building an online appointment platform for a group of 14 health clinics. The hardware kiosks for clinic lobbies are procured under a fixed-price contract with a predictive schedule. The patient web and mobile apps are built in two-week sprints. The sponsor is the group's operations director. Halfway through, a regional health authority publishes new rules on storing patient data. Clinic receptionists, who will use the system daily, have attended only one of six sprint reviews.
exhibits: Status at week 12: Kiosk contract: 2 of 4 milestones accepted. App: velocity 24, 26, 21, 22. Remaining backlog: 160 points. Budget: BAC 400,000; EV 180,000; AC 210,000; PV 200,000.

cases.title: Warehouse automation rollout
cases.body: Your company is installing automated picking robots in three warehouses over nine months. The project follows a predictive plan with phase gates. Warehouse staff are anxious about job changes, and the union has asked for a meeting. After installation in the first warehouse, picking speed improved only 5%, against a business case target of 25%. A supplier delay has used most of the schedule float on the second site.
exhibits: Risk register extract: R7 'Robot supplier delay' – probability 40%, impact 30 days – response: mitigate (secondary supplier pre-qualified).

questions.stem: A newly formed agile team is debating which features matter most, and each member argues from their own department's point of view. What should the project manager do first?
questions.explanation: A shared vision gives the team a common basis for decisions. Co-creating it with the product owner builds ownership and resolves departmental tunnel vision.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to rank the features and share the list
Facilitate a session with the team and product owner to create a shared product vision
Assign the most experienced developer to make feature decisions
Start the first sprint and let priorities emerge from velocity

rationales.A: Imposing a ranking skips alignment; the team still lacks a shared 'why'.
rationales.C: Delegating to one person bypasses collaboration and the product owner's role.
rationales.D: Starting without direction wastes effort; velocity does not set priorities.

questions.stem: Two functional leads repeatedly argue about test-environment time during status meetings, and the meetings now overrun. What is the BEST action for the project manager?
questions.explanation: Collaborating / problem-solving addresses the root cause and builds commitment. It is the preferred first approach.

options.text: Meet both leads together to understand their needs and agree a shared booking approach
Escalate the issue to their functional managers
Give priority to the lead whose work is on the critical path
Remove the topic from the status meeting agenda

rationales.B: Escalation is premature before the PM tries to resolve it.
rationales.C: Forcing a decision may be needed later but ignores the other lead's needs.
rationales.D: Withdrawing avoids the conflict without solving it.

questions.stem: During a retrospective, one developer becomes visibly upset after a teammate criticizes his code in front of everyone. What should the scrum master do?
questions.explanation: Psychological safety is essential. Using the team's own working agreement and following up privately addresses the behaviour without humiliating anyone.

options.text: Ask the developer to stay calm and continue the retrospective
End the retrospective early and report the incident to HR
Pause, remind the team of the working agreement on respectful feedback, and follow up privately with both people
Ignore it, as conflict is healthy in agile teams

rationales.A: Dismissing emotions damages psychological safety.
rationales.B: HR escalation is disproportionate for a first incident.
rationales.D: Healthy conflict is about ideas; this has become personal.

questions.stem: A team member has been late with their tasks for three sprints and seems disengaged in meetings. What should the project manager do first?
questions.explanation: Leaders give corrective attention privately and start by understanding the cause, which might be personal, skill-related or a blocker.

options.text: Raise the issue in the daily stand-up so the team can help
Meet privately with the team member to understand what is happening
Ask the functional manager to replace the team member
Reassign their stories to other team members

rationales.A: Public discussion can embarrass the person.
rationales.C: Replacement is premature without understanding the cause.
rationales.D: Reassigning treats the symptom only.

questions.stem: Your organization has started allowing generative-AI assistants for drafting project documents. A team member pasted confidential client requirements into a public AI tool. What should you do FIRST?
questions.explanation: Data exposure is a compliance and security incident. It must be reported and contained using the organization's procedures. Team norms for responsible AI use can follow.

options.text: Ban all AI tools for the team immediately
Report the incident according to the organization's data-protection procedure and contain the exposure
Ask the team member to delete their chat history and say nothing
Add an item to the lessons-learned register

rationales.A: A blanket ban may be considered later, but it does not address the exposure.
rationales.C: Concealing the incident breaches policy and ethics.
rationales.D: Lessons learned are useful, but not first.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions best demonstrate servant leadership by a project manager on an agile team?
questions.explanation: Servant leaders enable the team by removing impediments and protecting focus. Task assignment, approval gates and individual metrics undermine self-organization.

options.text: Removing an impediment the team cannot resolve themselves
Assigning daily tasks to each developer
Shielding the team from mid-sprint requests from outside stakeholders
Approving every technical design decision personally
Reporting each team member's velocity individually

rationales.A: Correct: removing impediments is a core servant-leader duty.
rationales.C: Correct: protecting the team's focus enables delivery.
rationales.D: Central approval creates a bottleneck.
rationales.E: Individual velocity encourages local optimization and gaming.

questions.stem: Three months into a construction project, the project manager learns that a local residents' association has concerns about noise. The association is not in the stakeholder register. What should the project manager do NEXT?
questions.explanation: Stakeholder identification is continuous. A newly found stakeholder is first recorded and analyzed so engagement can be planned.

options.text: Add the association to the stakeholder register and analyze its interest and influence
Send the association the project's noise permits
Ask the sponsor to deal with external groups
Continue as planned because the permits are already approved

rationales.B: Sending documents without analysis may not address the concern.
rationales.D: Ignoring an influential group risks delays.

questions.stem: A key business user rarely attends sprint reviews, and features delivered for her department have had low adoption. What is the BEST approach?
questions.explanation: Engagement must suit the stakeholder. Understanding her constraints and adapting the format (short demos, async video, a delegate) moves her from neutral to supportive.

options.text: Escalate her absence to the sponsor
Meet her to understand her constraints and agree a more convenient way to involve her in feedback
Stop building features for her department
Ask the product owner to accept the features on her behalf

rationales.A: Escalation before trying to engage damages the relationship.
rationales.C: Abandoning features ignores real business needs.
rationales.D: Acceptance without user input continues the adoption problem.

questions.stem: Marketing requires a product launch in June, but the compliance team states that mandatory controls cannot be ready until August. Both are powerful stakeholders. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Alignment means bringing conflicting stakeholders together around objectives and finding options. For example, a limited pilot could launch while the controls are completed. Genuine trade-offs go to the sponsor.

options.text: Proceed with the June launch and add the controls afterwards
Facilitate a joint meeting to explore options against business objectives and take the trade-off to the sponsor
Side with compliance because regulation always wins
Ask each stakeholder to submit a change request

rationales.A: Launching without mandatory controls breaches compliance.
rationales.C: Compliance must be met, but other options may satisfy both groups.
rationales.D: Change requests do not resolve the underlying conflict.

questions.stem: During a sprint review, the sponsor says she expected a feature that was never in the product backlog. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: In agile, new needs go into the product backlog, where the product owner prioritizes them against other value. This respects the sponsor's need without disrupting the sprint.

options.text: Promise to add it in the next sprint
Explain that the feature is out of scope and move on
Work with the product owner to discuss the need and, if valuable, add it to the backlog for prioritization
Ask the team to work overtime to include it in this sprint

rationales.A: The PM cannot promise; prioritization belongs to the product owner.
rationales.D: Overtime and mid-sprint scope changes are unsustainable.

questions.stem: A senior engineer who is the only expert on a legacy interface will leave the project in four weeks. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Tacit knowledge transfers best through people: pairing and shadowing. Documentation supports it but cannot capture judgment alone.

options.text: Ask the engineer to write complete documentation before leaving
Arrange pairing and shadowing with a successor, supported by key documentation
Request that HR extend the engineer's assignment
Add a risk to the register and accept it

rationales.A: Documentation alone misses tacit knowledge.
rationales.C: Extension may not be possible and only delays the problem.
rationales.D: Acceptance is passive when a mitigation is available.

questions.stem: A project team grows from 6 to 10 members. How many additional communication channels does this create?
questions.explanation: Channels = n(n−1)/2. For 6 people: 15. For 10 people: 45. Additional channels = 45 − 15 = 30.

rationales.A: 4 is just the extra people.
rationales.B: 15 is the original number of channels.
rationales.D: 45 is the new total, not the increase.

questions.stem: Team members in three countries complain that they learn about decisions late. Meetings are held in the head office's time zone. What should the project manager do FIRST?
questions.explanation: Revisit the communications plan with the people affected. Use a mix of pull (decision log), push and interactive methods, and set fair meeting times.

options.text: Review the communications management plan with the team and adjust channels, timing and a shared decision log
Require everyone to attend all meetings regardless of local time
Send a weekly summary email to the whole team
Escalate the time-zone problem to the PMO

rationales.C: Summaries help, but alone they may not fix the timing of decisions.
rationales.D: The PM can resolve this within their authority.

questions.stem: Match each conflict-resolution technique to its description.
questions.explanation: Collaborating gives the most durable solution. Compromise is lose-lose but workable. Smoothing preserves relationships temporarily. Forcing suits emergencies.

right.text: Each party gives up something to reach a partial solution
Emphasize areas of agreement over differences
Escalate every conflict to the sponsor
Impose one viewpoint, often for urgent or safety issues
Incorporate multiple viewpoints to reach consensus

questions.stem: Place each stakeholder in the most appropriate power/interest grid quadrant.
questions.explanation: High power and high interest: manage closely. High power and low interest: keep satisfied. Low power and high interest: keep informed. Low on both: monitor.

items.text: Project sponsor who approves funding and attends every steering meeting
CFO who signs off budget but rarely follows project details
End users eager for the new system but with no decision authority
Building facilities staff who are minimally affected

questions.stem: Arrange these stakeholder engagement activities in the order they are normally performed.
questions.explanation: Engagement follows identify → analyze → plan → engage → monitor, and repeats as new stakeholders appear.

questions.stem: The project charter has been approved, but team members describe the project's purpose very differently. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Interactive sessions build shared understanding. A document alone rarely creates a common vision.

options.text: Email the charter to the team again
Hold a kickoff workshop to walk through the business case, objectives and success criteria, and invite questions
Ask the sponsor to issue a memo to the team
Proceed; purposes become clear during execution

rationales.A: Pushing the document again is unlikely to change understanding.
rationales.D: Misunderstanding now causes rework later.

questions.stem: Testing shows the project will miss the milestone the customer expects next month. The customer has not been told. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Transparency and early communication of bad news maintain trust and give stakeholders time to decide.

options.text: Wait until the testing results are final
Inform the customer promptly with the impact, cause and recovery options
Ask the team to compress testing to protect the date
Report the milestone as 'at risk' only on the internal dashboard

rationales.A: Delay reduces the options available.
rationales.D: Hiding it from the customer erodes trust.

questions.stem: A highly skilled but new team member is unsure about a complex task. Using situational leadership, which style is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: Someone with some competence and variable confidence benefits from coaching: high direction plus high support.

options.text: Delegating
Supporting
Coaching
Directing

rationales.A: Delegating suits high competence and high commitment.
rationales.B: Supporting suits capable people with low confidence on familiar tasks.
rationales.D: Directing suits enthusiastic beginners with low skill.

questions.stem: Which THREE practices help transfer knowledge within and beyond an agile team?
questions.explanation: Pairing, communities of practice and accessible recordings spread knowledge. Private registers and single specialists create knowledge silos.

options.text: Pair programming
Communities of practice
Keeping the lessons-learned register private to the PM
Recording short demo videos for support staff
Assigning each component to one specialist only

questions.stem: Two business units want contradictory features in the next release. The product owner asks the project manager for help. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: The product owner owns prioritization. The PM facilitates by bringing the stakeholders together and making value transparent.

options.text: Decide which feature is more valuable
Facilitate a prioritization workshop with both units using agreed value criteria, so the product owner can decide
Build both features with half the effort each
Escalate to the sponsor immediately

rationales.A: Prioritization is the product owner's call.
rationales.C: Splitting effort usually delivers neither well.
rationales.D: Escalation comes after facilitation fails.

questions.stem: Which artifact is the BEST example of an information radiator?
questions.explanation: Information radiators are highly visible, current displays of progress, such as Kanban boards and burndown charts.

options.text: The communications management plan
A Kanban board displayed where the team and stakeholders can see it
A monthly status report emailed to sponsors
The stakeholder register

rationales.A: A plan is not a live display.
rationales.D: The register is not a progress display and may hold sensitive data.

questions.stem: Mid-project, the organization announces a sustainability commitment to cut emissions by 30%. How should the project manager handle the project vision?
questions.explanation: The vision must stay aligned with organizational strategy. The July 2026 outline emphasizes sustainability and value. Updating the vision is done openly, with the sponsor.

options.text: Ignore it, as the charter was already approved
Work with the sponsor to assess the impact and, if needed, update the vision and success criteria to include sustainability outcomes
Add a sustainability slide to the next status report
Wait for the next project to adopt it

rationales.A: Strategy changes can invalidate the charter's assumptions.
rationales.D: Waiting misses alignment with strategy.

questions.stem: A safety inspector and the site supervisor disagree about whether scaffolding can be used today. Work is due to start in one hour. Which conflict approach is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Safety issues justify a directive (forcing) approach. Safety always takes precedence; the underlying disagreement can be resolved afterwards.

options.text: Compromise: use the scaffolding for half the day
Force: follow the safety inspector's decision until the issue is resolved
Smooth: emphasize shared goals and proceed
Withdraw: let them sort it out

rationales.A: Partial use is still unsafe.
rationales.D: Withdrawing leaves risk unmanaged.

questions.stem: A project will build a regulated medical device with a companion mobile app. Device requirements are fixed by regulation; app features depend on user feedback. Which delivery approach is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: Hybrid combines approaches based on each component's uncertainty and constraints.

options.text: Predictive for the whole project
Agile for the whole project
Hybrid: predictive for the device, iterative and incremental for the app
Wait until all app requirements are known

rationales.A: Predictive suits the device but slows app learning.
rationales.B: Agile alone may conflict with regulatory documentation and gates.
rationales.D: Waiting delays value and learning.

questions.stem: Which items make up the performance measurement baseline?
questions.explanation: The performance measurement baseline integrates the scope, schedule and cost baselines. Management reserve is not part of it.

options.text: Scope, schedule and cost baselines
Scope baseline, risk register and quality plan
Cost baseline and management reserve
Project charter and project management plan

rationales.B: The risk register and quality plan are not baselines.
rationales.C: Management reserve sits outside the baseline.
rationales.D: The charter authorizes; it is not a baseline.

questions.stem: A developer adds an extra dashboard widget that the customer did not request, believing it will please them. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Gold plating means adding features beyond requirements without a request. It adds risk and cost and is discouraged.

options.text: Scope creep
Gold plating
Progressive elaboration
Value engineering

rationales.A: Scope creep is uncontrolled change, usually from stakeholders.
rationales.C: Progressive elaboration is adding detail as information emerges.
rationales.D: Value engineering seeks the same function at lower cost.

questions.stem: The customer inspected the completed deliverables and formally signed acceptance. Which process does this represent?
questions.explanation: Validate scope is formal customer acceptance of deliverables. Control quality (verification of correctness) normally happens before it.

options.text: Control quality
Validate scope
Close project
Control scope

rationales.A: Control quality checks correctness internally.
rationales.C: Closing comes after acceptance of all deliverables.
rationales.D: Control scope monitors scope and changes.

questions.stem: Arrange these scope management activities in the typical predictive order.
questions.explanation: Predictive scope work moves from requirements to scope statement, WBS decomposition, then ongoing validation and control.

questions.stem: Stakeholders want all twelve planned reports delivered together at the end of the project. Usage of the current reporting system is unknown. What should the project manager recommend?
questions.explanation: Value-based delivery releases the highest-value items early to gain feedback and value sooner. This often reveals unneeded scope.

options.text: Deliver all twelve reports together as requested
Release the two highest-value reports first, measure usage and adjust the backlog
Ask the team to estimate all twelve in detail first
Cancel the reporting scope

rationales.A: Big-bang delivery delays value and feedback.
rationales.C: Detailed upfront estimates add little value under uncertainty.
rationales.D: Cancelling ignores a legitimate need.

questions.stem: Which TWO measures best indicate that a project is delivering business value rather than just outputs?
questions.explanation: Outcome measures such as adoption and process improvement show value. Output counts do not.

options.text: Number of features completed
Increase in customer adoption rate
Lines of code written
Reduction in processing time for the target business process
Hours logged by the team

questions.stem: A critical specialist is over-allocated across two activities in the same week, and both activities have float. Which technique should be used FIRST?
questions.explanation: Resource smoothing reschedules within available float, so the critical path is not affected. Use it before levelling, which may extend the project.

options.text: Resource levelling
Resource smoothing
Crashing
Fast tracking

rationales.A: Levelling can change the end date; use it if smoothing is insufficient.
rationales.C: Crashing adds resources to shorten duration.
rationales.D: Fast tracking overlaps activities to save time.

questions.stem: A functional manager reassigns a key team member to another project without notice. What should the project manager do FIRST?
questions.explanation: In a matrix organization the PM negotiates resources with functional managers first; escalation comes later if needed.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor
Meet the functional manager to understand the reason and negotiate a solution
Hire a contractor immediately
Update the schedule to show the delay

rationales.A: Escalation before negotiation harms relationships.
rationales.C: Hiring may be unnecessary and is not first.
rationales.D: Re-planning happens after the situation is understood.

questions.stem: The scope of work for a vendor is well defined and stable, and the buyer wants to minimize its own cost risk. Which contract type is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: With a clear, stable scope, firm fixed price places most cost risk on the seller.

options.text: Cost plus fixed fee
Time and materials
Firm fixed price
Cost plus award fee

rationales.A: Cost-reimbursable contracts put risk on the buyer.
rationales.B: T&M suits small or undefined work.
rationales.D: Award-fee contracts are cost-reimbursable.

questions.stem: A seller claims additional payment because, it says, the buyer changed requirements. The buyer disagrees. What is the PREFERRED way to resolve this?
questions.explanation: Contested changes (claims) should be settled by negotiation following the contract's terms. Alternative dispute resolution or litigation are later options.

options.text: Take the seller to court
Negotiate according to the contract's claims administration process
Withhold all payments until the seller drops the claim
Terminate the contract

rationales.A: Litigation is a last resort.
rationales.C: Withholding payment may breach the contract.
rationales.D: Termination is extreme and costly.

questions.stem: Match each procurement document to its purpose.
questions.explanation: RFI gathers information, RFQ requests prices, RFP requests proposals, and the SOW describes the work.

right.text: Describe the work to be performed
Request price quotes for well-defined items

questions.stem: BAC = 200,000. EV = 80,000. AC = 100,000. PV = 90,000. What is the cost performance index (CPI)?
questions.explanation: CPI = EV / AC = 80,000 / 100,000 = 0.80. The project is over budget.

rationales.D: 1.25 is AC/EV.

questions.stem: Using the same data (BAC 200,000, EV 80,000, AC 100,000), what is the estimate at completion if current cost performance continues?

rationales.A: 220,000 is AC + (BAC − EV).
rationales.D: That is the BAC, which assumes no variance.

questions.stem: Where is the contingency reserve for identified risks held?
questions.explanation: Contingency reserves (for known-unknowns) are part of the cost baseline. Management reserve (unknown-unknowns) is outside it.

options.text: Outside the cost baseline, controlled by management
Inside the cost baseline
In the procurement budget
In the management reserve

rationales.A: That describes management reserve.
rationales.D: Management reserve is for unknown-unknowns.

questions.stem: An activity has optimistic 6, most likely 9 and pessimistic 18 days. What is the PERT (beta) estimate?

options.text: 9 days
10 days
11 days
12 days

rationales.A: 9 is the most likely value only.
rationales.D: Not a valid result.

questions.stem: A control chart shows seven consecutive measurements above the mean, all within the control limits. What should the project manager conclude?
questions.explanation: The 'rule of seven': seven consecutive points on one side of the mean suggests a non-random pattern that needs investigation.

options.text: The process is in control; no action is needed
The process may be out of control and should be investigated
The control limits should be widened
The specification limits have been exceeded

rationales.A: Points within limits can still show a non-random trend.
rationales.D: No information about specification limits is given.

questions.stem: Classify each cost as a cost of conformance or a cost of non-conformance.
questions.explanation: Prevention (training) and appraisal (inspection, testing) are conformance costs. Internal and external failures (rework, warranty, lost business) are non-conformance costs.

questions.stem: A team keeps finding defects during the sprint review that should have been caught earlier. What is the BEST way to prevent this?
questions.explanation: Agile builds quality in. A stronger definition of done prevents defects instead of finding them late.

options.text: Add a separate testing sprint after every two development sprints
Strengthen the definition of done to include automated tests and peer review
Ask the product owner to stop accepting stories
Extend the sprint by a week

rationales.A: Separate test sprints delay feedback (a 'mini waterfall').
rationales.C: Withholding acceptance does not fix the cause.
rationales.D: Longer sprints do not fix the process.

questions.stem: The project is three weeks behind schedule. The sponsor will not approve more budget but accepts some additional risk. Which compression technique fits BEST?
questions.explanation: Fast tracking overlaps activities. It adds risk rather than cost, which matches the sponsor's constraints.

options.text: Crashing
Fast tracking
Resource levelling
Reducing scope without approval

rationales.A: Crashing adds cost.
rationales.D: Scope changes need approval.

questions.stem: Activity A (4 days) precedes B (6 days) and C (3 days). B and C both precede D (2 days). What is the critical path duration?
questions.explanation: Paths: A-B-D = 4 + 6 + 2 = 12; A-C-D = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9. The longest is 12 days.

options.text: 9 days
12 days
15 days
13 days

rationales.A: 9 is the shorter path.
rationales.C: 15 is the sum of all activities.
rationales.D: Not a valid path.

questions.stem: An agile team's velocity over the last four sprints was 30, 34, 28 and 32 points. 192 points remain in the release, and the team only releases at sprint ends. How many more sprints should the forecast show?
questions.explanation: Average velocity = 31 points. 192 / 31 ≈ 6.2 sprints. Because work completes only at sprint boundaries, the forecast is 7 sprints. Present it as a range (6–7) to stakeholders.

rationales.A: 5 sprints would need about 38 points per sprint.
rationales.B: 6 sprints delivers only about 186 points, short of 192.
rationales.D: 8 is overly pessimistic given stable velocity.

questions.stem: A cumulative flow diagram shows the 'In test' band widening every week while 'Done' grows slowly. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A widening band means work is accumulating in that state: a bottleneck. Limiting WIP and swarming on testing are typical responses.

options.text: The team is highly productive
A bottleneck in testing
Scope is decreasing
The backlog needs more stories

rationales.A: Accumulating WIP is not productivity.
rationales.C: Scope is shown by the total height.
rationales.D: The backlog is not the constraint.

questions.stem: Status reports show green for six months, but the integration test reveals major defects. The sponsor asks why. What should the project manager do going forward?
questions.explanation: Honest, metric-based reporting prevents 'watermelon' status and supports timely decisions.

options.text: Keep reporting green to avoid alarming the sponsor
Base status on objective measures such as test results and earned value, and report risks transparently
Stop issuing status reports
Blame the test team for late testing

rationales.A: This repeats the problem.
rationales.D: Blame does not fix reporting.

questions.stem: The project's final deliverable is accepted. One vendor contract still has an open punch-list item. What should the project manager do before closing the project?
questions.explanation: Procurements must be closed (all work complete and claims settled) before the project is closed.

options.text: Close the project and handle the vendor later
Complete procurement closure by resolving the open item and confirming contract completion
Transfer the open item to operations
Archive the contract file

rationales.A: Leaving contracts open creates liability.
rationales.C: Contract obligations remain with the project.
rationales.D: Archiving doesn't resolve the open item.

questions.stem: The sponsor terminates the project because of a strategic merger. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Terminated projects still go through closure to protect the organization and preserve knowledge.

options.text: Release the team immediately and stop all activity
Follow closure procedures: document status, close contracts, archive work, capture lessons learned and release resources
Keep working quietly in case the decision changes
Ask the team to finish their current tasks

rationales.A: Stopping abruptly loses knowledge and leaves obligations open.
rationales.D: Further work is not authorized.

questions.stem: Which THREE activities belong to project closure?
questions.explanation: Closure confirms acceptance, finalizes lessons learned and transitions the product. The WBS and charter are created in planning and initiation.

options.text: Obtain final acceptance of deliverables
Create the WBS
Finalize the lessons-learned register
Transfer the product to operations
Develop the project charter

questions.stem: Which event formally marks the start of execution and aligns the team and stakeholders on the plan?
questions.explanation: The kickoff meeting launches the project or a major phase and aligns everyone on objectives, roles and plans.

options.text: Sprint retrospective
Kickoff meeting
Phase gate review
Lessons-learned session

rationales.A: Retrospectives look back.
rationales.D: Lessons sessions capture learning.

questions.stem: Match each earned value formula to what it calculates.
questions.explanation: CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV; CPI = EV / AC; EAC = BAC / CPI when current performance continues.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a minimum viable product (MVP)?
questions.explanation: An MVP tests assumptions about value with real users as early as possible.

options.text: Deliver the full scope at the lowest cost
Test a value hypothesis with the smallest useful release to gain feedback
Satisfy contractual milestones
Produce a prototype that will be thrown away

rationales.A: MVP is not full scope.
rationales.C: Milestones may differ from value hypotheses.
rationales.D: An MVP is usable, not necessarily throwaway.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps of building a project budget in order.
questions.explanation: Costs roll up from activities to work packages and control accounts. Contingency makes the cost baseline; management reserve completes the project budget.

items.text: Aggregate to work-package and control-account costs
Add management reserve to form the total budget
Add contingency reserves to form the cost baseline

questions.stem: An agile organization wants to maximize team performance on a long-running product. Which staffing approach is BEST?
questions.explanation: Stable, dedicated, cross-functional teams build trust, shared knowledge and predictable velocity.

options.text: Reassign developers every sprint based on availability
Keep a stable, dedicated, cross-functional team
Use specialists from a central pool per task
Rotate the product owner weekly

rationales.A: Frequent reassignment destroys team learning.
rationales.D: Product ownership needs continuity.

questions.stem: A decision about a 500,000 vendor contract is above the project manager's authority. Two stakeholders are pressing for a quick decision. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Governance defines decision rights. The PM supports the decision with analysis and follows the escalation path.

options.text: Make the decision to keep the project moving
Prepare options and impacts, and take the decision to the steering committee per the governance framework
Let the two stakeholders decide between themselves
Delay the decision until the next phase

rationales.A: Exceeding authority breaches governance.
rationales.D: Delay may harm the project.

questions.stem: In which organizational structure does the project manager typically have the MOST authority?
questions.explanation: In projectized organizations the PM controls budget and resources. Authority is lowest in functional organizations.

options.text: Functional
Weak matrix
Balanced matrix
Projectized

rationales.A: Functional: authority sits with functional managers.
rationales.B: Weak matrix: the PM is more of a coordinator.

questions.stem: Match each PMO type to its level of control.
questions.explanation: PMO types range from supportive (low control) to controlling (moderate) to directive (high).

right.text: Provides templates and training; low control
Requires compliance with frameworks; moderate control

questions.stem: Midway through a CRM rollout, a new data-protection regulation takes effect that requires explicit consent tracking. What should the project manager do FIRST?
questions.explanation: First understand the regulatory requirements with experts, then plan the change (backlog, change control, risk updates).

options.text: Ignore it until the next release
Engage the compliance or privacy officer to assess the impact and requirements
Add consent tracking directly to the current sprint
Ask the vendor to absorb the change

rationales.A: Non-compliance is not optional.
rationales.C: Acting before understanding may produce the wrong solution.
rationales.D: Contract terms decide who pays; this is not the first step.

questions.stem: A tester finds that the release does not meet mandatory accessibility requirements. The release date is tomorrow. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Mandatory requirements are not negotiable trade-offs. Raise the issue transparently and follow policy.

options.text: Release and fix accessibility in a later patch
Inform the product owner and stakeholders, and do not release until the compliance gap is resolved or formally handled per policy
Ask the tester to mark the issue as minor
Release only to internal users without telling anyone

rationales.A: Knowingly releasing non-compliant software breaches obligations.
rationales.D: Concealment is unethical.

questions.stem: A sponsor asks a developer directly to add a new report. The developer tells the project manager. What should the project manager do FIRST?
questions.explanation: In a predictive project, changes are logged and their impact analyzed before the CCB or decision maker decides.

options.text: Tell the developer to add the report
Log a change request and evaluate its impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk
Refuse the request
Ask the change control board to approve it immediately

rationales.A: Implementing before approval bypasses change control.
rationales.D: The CCB needs an impact analysis first.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps of handling a change request in a predictive project.
questions.explanation: Integrated change control: log → analyze → decide → update → communicate.

items.text: Update plans and baselines if approved
Submit to the change control board for decision

questions.stem: In an agile project, where should a newly requested feature normally go?
questions.explanation: Agile welcomes change through the product backlog. The product owner orders it by value.

options.text: Into the current sprint immediately
Into the product backlog for the product owner to prioritize
To the change control board
Into the risk register

rationales.A: Changing a sprint mid-way disrupts the sprint goal.
rationales.C: Agile rarely uses a CCB for backlog changes.
rationales.D: A feature request is not a risk.

questions.stem: In every sprint the team loses two days waiting for database access approvals from another department. What should the scrum master do?
questions.explanation: Servant leaders remove impediments beyond the team's control, using data to make the case.

options.text: Ask the team to plan less work
Escalate the impediment with data on lost time and work with the department to streamline approvals
Tell the team to use production credentials
Record it in the retrospective and accept it

rationales.A: This hides the root cause.
rationales.D: Accepting a recurring blocker is passive.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between an issue and a risk?
questions.explanation: Risks are uncertain and in the future. Issues are current problems that need resolution.

options.text: Issues are always larger than risks
An issue has occurred; a risk is an uncertain future event
Risks are only negative; issues can be positive
Issues are owned by the sponsor; risks by the PM

rationales.A: Size is not the distinction.
rationales.D: Ownership varies.

questions.stem: A risk has a 25% probability and a cost impact of 80,000. What is its expected monetary value?
questions.explanation: EMV = probability × impact = 0.25 × (−80,000) = −20,000.

rationales.D: Not a valid result.

questions.stem: Classify each risk response as a threat response or an opportunity response.
questions.explanation: Threats: avoid, transfer, mitigate (and accept, escalate). Opportunities: exploit, share, enhance (and accept, escalate).

questions.stem: The project buys insurance to cover possible equipment damage during shipping. Which risk response is this?
questions.explanation: Insurance shifts the financial impact to a third party: transfer.

options.text: Avoid
Transfer
Mitigate
Accept

rationales.A: Avoid removes the threat entirely, e.g. by not shipping.
rationales.C: Mitigate reduces probability or impact, e.g. better packing.
rationales.D: Accept means no proactive action.

questions.stem: An identified risk occurs, and the planned response is carried out. What should the project manager do NEXT?
questions.explanation: After implementing a response, monitor its effectiveness and update the registers for residual and secondary risks.

options.text: Close the risk register
Monitor the response's effectiveness and check for secondary or residual risks
Create a new project charter
Request management reserve

rationales.A: The register stays active.
rationales.D: Contingency funds the planned response; management reserve is for unknowns.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about using AI forecasting tools on a project are MOST accurate?
questions.explanation: AI can improve forecasting but adds risks (bias, hallucination, data leakage). People stay accountable for decisions.

options.text: AI forecasts remove the need for risk management
AI tools can introduce risks such as biased or inaccurate outputs that need validation
AI-generated estimates should be reviewed by accountable humans before decisions
AI tools are always compliant with data-protection rules
AI outputs do not need to be documented

questions.stem: A retrospective shows code reviews wait two days on average. What should happen next?
questions.explanation: Continuous improvement follows PDCA: plan a change, do it, check the effect, act on the result.

options.text: Record the finding for future projects
The team agrees a concrete improvement action, tries it in the next sprint and checks the result
The PM mandates that reviews must be done within one hour
Escalate to management

rationales.A: Improvement should apply now, not only later.
rationales.D: The team can solve this itself.

questions.stem: Which Lean concept refers to eliminating activities that add no value for the customer?
questions.explanation: Lean focuses on removing waste, such as waiting, handoffs, defects and over-processing, to increase flow.

options.text: Kaizen
Waste (muda) reduction
Gold plating
Crashing

rationales.A: Kaizen is the philosophy of continuous small improvement.
rationales.D: Crashing adds resources.

questions.stem: A new procurement system went live a month ago, but most staff still use the old spreadsheets. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Low adoption is a people-change problem. Reinforcement, training and champions (as in ADKAR) drive adoption.

options.text: Ask IT to add more features
Apply change management: identify champions, provide hands-on training, communicate benefits and retire the old spreadsheets
Report that the project is complete
Escalate the staff to HR

rationales.A: More features don't address adoption.
rationales.D: Punitive action increases resistance.

questions.stem: Arrange the ADKAR change model elements in order.
questions.explanation: ADKAR: Awareness of the need, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how, Ability to implement, Reinforcement to sustain.

questions.stem: A competitor launches a free product with similar features to the one your team is building. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: External changes can affect the business case. Assess the impact and let the right decision makers adjust direction.

options.text: Continue the plan; the charter is approved
Facilitate a rapid impact assessment with the product owner and sponsor to revisit priorities and the business case
Cancel the project immediately
Copy the competitor's features

rationales.A: Ignoring market change risks delivering no value.
rationales.C: Cancellation is not the PM's unilateral decision.
rationales.D: Copying is not a strategy.

questions.stem: Match each external factor to its PESTLE category.
questions.explanation: PESTLE groups external influences so their impact on the project can be assessed systematically.

questions.stem: The organization requires all projects to report their carbon footprint at phase gates. The vendor cannot provide emissions data. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Sustainability reporting is an organizational compliance requirement. Manage the gap transparently with a defensible method.

options.text: Skip the requirement for this project
Treat it as a compliance requirement: log the gap as an issue, work with the vendor on estimation methods, and inform governance
Estimate a number without a method
Replace the vendor immediately

rationales.A: Requirements cannot be skipped unilaterally.
rationales.D: Replacement is drastic and may not be needed.

questions.stem: Portfolio leaders want visibility of several agile teams without adding heavy reporting. What governance approach fits BEST?
questions.explanation: Adaptive governance uses transparency and frequent review events rather than heavy documentation.

options.text: Weekly 20-page status reports from each team
Lightweight governance using shared roadmaps, portfolio Kanban and regular review events
A phase-gate approval before every sprint
No governance, because agile teams are self-organizing

rationales.A: Heavy reporting slows delivery.
rationales.D: Some governance is always needed.

questions.stem: A problem keeps recurring even though the team applies the same workaround each time. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Recurring issues call for root cause analysis to prevent recurrence.

options.text: Continue applying the workaround
Perform root cause analysis, such as 5 whys or a fishbone diagram, and address the cause
Add more workaround documentation
Accept the issue

rationales.A: Workarounds treat symptoms.
rationales.D: Accepting is passive.

questions.stem: Given the new patient-data rules, what should you do FIRST?
questions.explanation: Understand the regulatory impact with experts before deciding on backlog items, contract changes or a pause.

options.text: Pause the whole project
Engage the organization's privacy or compliance lead to assess the impact on both app and kiosk scope
Ask the kiosk vendor to absorb any change
Add a generic 'compliance' story to the backlog

rationales.A: Pausing is premature.
rationales.D: A vague story without analysis won't ensure compliance.

questions.stem: Based on the exhibit, what is the cost performance index (CPI), and what does it mean?
questions.explanation: CPI = EV / AC = 180,000 / 210,000 ≈ 0.86. Less than 1 means over budget.

options.text: 0.86: over budget
0.90: behind schedule
1.17: under budget
0.86: ahead of schedule

rationales.B: 0.90 is SPI (EV/PV), which shows schedule, not cost.
rationales.D: CPI is about cost, not schedule.

questions.stem: Receptionists rarely attend sprint reviews. What is the BEST way to improve their engagement?
questions.explanation: Adapting engagement to the stakeholders' working reality raises participation and feedback quality.

options.text: Report their absence to clinic managers
Hold short reviews in the clinics at quiet times, or use recorded demos with a quick feedback form
Have the product owner accept stories for them
Wait until user acceptance testing

rationales.A: Escalation without adapting is unlikely to help.
rationales.D: Late feedback is expensive.

questions.stem: The kiosk vendor says the new rules require encrypted storage not in the contract. Which TWO actions are appropriate?
questions.explanation: Contract changes go through the agreed change process with an impact assessment. Unilateral demands or switching contract types are inappropriate.

options.text: Follow the contract's change control process to evaluate and agree the change
Tell the vendor to make the change at no cost because regulation is their problem
Assess the impact of the change on the kiosk milestones and budget
Switch to a cost-reimbursable contract immediately
Ignore the kiosks; only the apps store patient data

questions.stem: Picking speed improved only 5% at the first site. Staff report they still pick some orders manually 'to be safe'. What is the MOST likely focus for improvement?
questions.explanation: Benefits depend on adoption. The symptoms point to people and process change rather than technology.

options.text: Buy faster robots
Organizational change support: training, reinforcement and involving staff in process redesign
Cancel the remaining rollouts
Change the business case target

rationales.A: The technology may not be the problem.
rationales.D: Changing the target hides the problem.

questions.stem: The union has requested a meeting. What should you do?
questions.explanation: The union is a high-influence stakeholder. Engaging directly and transparently, with HR involved, reduces resistance.

options.text: Decline, because HR handles unions
Accept, with HR, to listen to concerns and share plans transparently, then update the stakeholder engagement plan
Send a written FAQ instead
Ask the sponsor to cancel the meeting

rationales.A: Avoiding a key stakeholder increases risk.
rationales.D: Cancelling damages trust.

questions.stem: The supplier delay risk (R7) has now occurred. What should you do?
questions.explanation: When an identified risk occurs, carry out its planned response and update the registers. It is now an issue.

options.text: Create a new risk response from scratch
Implement the planned response (engage the pre-qualified secondary supplier) and update the risk register and issue log
Wait to see whether the supplier recovers
Use management reserve to pay for overtime

rationales.A: A response already exists.
rationales.D: Overtime is not the planned response, and management reserve is for unknowns.

questions.stem: The final site is accepted. Order these closing steps.
questions.explanation: Accept → close procurements → transition → lessons and archive → release resources. Some steps may overlap, but this sequence protects the organization.

items.text: Finalize lessons learned and archive records
Obtain formal acceptance of the final deliverables
Transfer support to the operations team

questions.stem: At release planning, the product owner and the head of sales disagree on what 'done' means for a reporting feature. What should the project manager do FIRST?
questions.explanation: Explicit, agreed acceptance criteria align expectations before work starts and prevent rework at the review.

options.text: Use the product owner's definition because they own the backlog
Facilitate a session to agree explicit acceptance criteria for the feature with both parties
Ask the team to build both versions
Escalate to the sponsor for a ruling

rationales.A: Ownership of priority does not remove the need to align acceptance criteria with key stakeholders.
rationales.D: Escalation is premature before facilitation.

questions.stem: A steering committee member keeps asking for detailed weekly reports, while the agile team already publishes a live dashboard. The member says the dashboard 'is hard to read'. What is the BEST response?
questions.explanation: Managing expectations starts with understanding the stakeholder's real information needs, then tailoring the format without adding waste.

options.text: Produce the detailed weekly report as requested
Meet the member to understand what decisions they need to make and adapt the dashboard or provide a short tailored summary
Tell the member the dashboard is the agile standard
Remove the member from the distribution list

rationales.A: This may add effort without meeting the underlying need.
rationales.D: Excluding a governance stakeholder is inappropriate.

questions.stem: Only one developer understands the payment module, and the team's velocity drops whenever she is away. Which action BEST addresses this?
questions.explanation: Pairing and story rotation spread tacit knowledge and remove a single point of failure. This is collective code ownership.

options.text: Ask her to document the module fully
Introduce pairing and rotate payment stories across team members
Hire a contractor specialist as a backup
Add the risk to the register and accept it

rationales.A: Documentation helps but rarely transfers tacit knowledge.
rationales.D: Acceptance ignores an easy, effective response.

questions.stem: A release burnup chart shows the completed-work line rising steadily, but the total-scope line is rising just as fast. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A burnup chart shows scope separately. If scope grows as fast as completion, the lines never meet; the product owner must re-plan or reprioritize.

options.text: The team's velocity is too low
Scope is growing at about the same rate as work is completed, so the release date is at risk
The project is on track
The chart is incorrectly configured

rationales.A: Velocity looks steady; scope growth is the problem.
rationales.D: This is a normal and useful burnup pattern.

questions.stem: Retrospective actions are agreed each sprint but rarely implemented. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Continuous improvement needs few, visible, owned actions that are checked (PDCA). Putting them in the backlog makes them real work.

options.text: Stop holding retrospectives
Limit improvements to one or two actions, add them to the backlog with owners and review them at the next retrospective
Assign all improvement actions to the scrum master
Report the team to management

rationales.A: Removing retrospectives removes learning.
rationales.D: Punitive action discourages honesty.

questions.stem: Midway through a hybrid project, a new trade tariff raises the cost of imported hardware by 20%. What should the project manager do FIRST?
questions.explanation: External changes are analyzed for impact on the business case before decisions. The sponsor or governance body decides on options.

options.text: Absorb the cost using management reserve
Assess the impact on budget, schedule and business case and inform the sponsor with options
Switch suppliers immediately
Ask the team to reduce scope to compensate

rationales.A: Using reserve needs approval and analysis first.
rationales.C: Switching without analysis may add risk.
rationales.D: Scope changes need stakeholder decisions.

questions.stem: A new AI service appears that could automate a large part of the product the team is building. What is the MOST appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Technology shifts are external environment changes. A time-boxed spike gives evidence for the product owner and sponsor to decide.

options.text: Ignore it until the project ends
Facilitate a quick spike to assess the service, and review the backlog and business case with the product owner
Cancel the project
Integrate the service immediately

rationales.A: Ignoring the change risks building obsolete features.
rationales.C: Cancelling is not the PM's unilateral decision.
rationales.D: Integrating without assessment adds risk (security, cost, compliance).

questions.stem: Your organization requires all new projects to report expected carbon emissions at the business-case gate. Where should this be addressed FIRST?
questions.explanation: Sustainability requirements shape the plan from the start: objectives, metrics, procurement choices and reporting. The July 2026 outline adds sustainability to project scenarios.

options.text: In the closure report
In planning: add sustainability objectives and metrics to the project management plan and business case
Only if the sponsor asks
In the lessons-learned register

rationales.A: Too late to influence decisions.
rationales.D: Lessons learned don't meet the requirement.

questions.stem: A team wants to use a generative-AI tool to summarize customer interviews. Which TWO actions should come FIRST?
questions.explanation: Using AI on personal data is a compliance question first: follow policy and protect personal data (consent, anonymization) before any processing.

options.text: Check the organization's AI and data-protection policies
Upload the interviews to test the tool's quality
Confirm customer consent or anonymize data as required
Let each team member choose their own tool
Skip review because the summaries are internal

questions.stem: A team member uses an AI coding assistant and submits code that contains a security flaw. How should the team prevent this in future?
questions.explanation: Humans remain accountable for AI-assisted output. Building checks into the definition of done applies the control consistently to everyone.

options.text: Ban AI tools
Add security review and automated scanning of all code, including AI-assisted code, to the definition of done
Make the team member responsible for all security checks
Rely on the AI tool's own warnings

rationales.A: Bans may be unnecessary and lose productivity.
rationales.D: Tool warnings are not sufficient assurance.

questions.stem: Benefits analysis shows a delivered feature is rarely used, while users ask for an improvement to another feature. What should the team do?
questions.explanation: Value-based delivery uses outcome data to change priorities and stops investing in low-value features.

options.text: Continue enhancing the unused feature as planned
Reprioritize the backlog toward the requested improvement and consider retiring the unused feature
Wait until the end of the project to decide
Ask users to use the feature more

rationales.A: Planned work that adds no value is waste.
